On today's stock market crash:

As an investor, on days like today, you have to ask yourself one question: What fundamentally changed over the last 24 hours?

The shift in the fundamental backdrop cannot be attributed solely to the Midterm Election results; markets had already largely priced in the outcome.

So, what changed between yesterday and today? What is the fundamental reason for today's decline?

One of the most likely catalysts is growing concern about a potential "ban" on AI, or at the very least, severe regulation of the industry.

Over the last 24 hours, Democratic lawmakers have publicly called for restrictions on advanced AI development, including an outright "ban on artificial superintelligence."

Frankly, an outright ban will not happen.

Such a ban, if even possible to enforce, would effectively mean the US surrendering its position in the global AI race to China.

Does this mean AI is "over" or today's stock market crash marks "the end?" Absolutely not.

Rather, we believe we are witnessing a sudden shift in sentiment colliding with excessive levels of leverage, potentially triggering forced liquidations by several major institutional investors.

Therefore, today's downturn is more technical than fundamental. This is not to discount the concerns around regulation, they are legitimate. But price action right now does not look orderly or rational.

We are in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in human history.

Zoom out and remain calm.

Again, people have this unrealistic fetish for closing exact tops, or buying exact bottoms. They imagine the pro trader who never loses and times everything perfectly. 

Reality is far from it.

Trading is a game of averages.

If my average purchase price is lower, and my average sell is higher I will out-compound you.

Timing the exact bottom is a fools errand, shorting is for risk management, not for PnL.

You short and close in profit so you have more cash on days like today. Would I have loved to be short into it? Sure, it would have been an extra +7% or so on our book. That doesn't matter as much as NOT LOSING money, managing your risk and preserving optionality. The sooner you understand this, the more profitable you'll become.

There were a plethora of posts on the timeline yesterday celebrating $STRC returning back to par.

I still believe Strategy is no longer a Bitcoin company.

It's a dividend company.

And $MSTR is nothing more than a piggy bank in the ponzi that Saylor uses to fund dividends.

Notice how BTC Yield has been down only since June, despite both the reserves and the price of BTC going higher.

This was THE metric they used to define success and shareholder value for MSTR... e.g. when they could sell more shares of MSTR to buy more Bitcoin and it be accretive rather than dilutive... until it stopped working.

Then they made up a new metric with new numbers for what's actually accretive and dilutive and never mentioned it again.

They currently have ~$4.9B of cash in their reserves.

How did they get it?

- primarily by selling billions of dollars of MSTR atm while it was still dilutive to shareholders

And remember, they've also REPURCHASED $2B of STRC while it was at a discount.

I actually think that's smart!

But, remember the preferred stock is what got them into this mess in the first place...

And now that it's back to par, they're simply going to add back to the debt by issuing more STRC to buy more Bitcoin which adds back to the dividends, obligations, ad infintum.

Not to mention, there's a big chance $MSTR itself is about to see billions of dollars in sell pressure if its removed from MSCI indices.

While I don't see there being a situation anywhere in the near term they'll be forced to sell their entire Bitcoin stack if the price goes low enough, I do think it's obvious they've shown they care much more about protecting the dividend than they do preserving accrual of BTC for the average shareholder... which is what the initial purpose of the company was supposed to be.

So I still encourage anyone who buys MSTR because they're bullish on Bitcoin to reconsider.

If you're bullish on Bitcoin, don't buy a stock that can be printed infinitely to pay someone else.

Just buy more Bitcoin.

"Don't trust, verify."

For some reason, we apply this logic to blockchains but not AI models.

Imagine this: you're paying for a specific AI model through an API, while the provider runs a lower-precision version or limits its capabilities.

It's why @miranetwork built Sterling, an AI inference platform that independently verifies whether providers are serving the models and capabilities they claim.

It runs five checks:

→ Model identity
→ Tool calls
→ Parameters honoured
→ Silent failures
→ Declared context window

Then Mira publishes the verification scores, and Sterling uses them to route requests to providers that pass its checks.

At launch, users can access Claude, GPT, and Gemini models through Sterling, with up to 50% off select models and payment options in USDC or $MIRA.

If verification is the standard in crypto, I think it should be the standard for AI providers, too.

You can try Sterling yourself here: https://t.co/dFLftPJAbf

thread_tweets.text:
AI’s power demand keeps outrunning the forecasts.

Data centers used under 5% of US electricity in 2024. Berkeley Lab now projects as much as 15% by 2030, and EPRI as much as 17%.  

Requests for power are moving even faster. In Texas the queue of data centers and other large power users waiting to connect grew from 63 GW to 474 GW in about 18 months.

The capacity being built for that demand will run around the clock for decades. Even GPUs from compute providers that fail under their debt tend to be bought by larger cloud companies and kept running.

AI is not the only new load. Only about 20% of GE Vernova’s contracted turbine capacity is tied explicitly to data centers.

U.S. electricity demand barely moved for fifteen years and is now climbing again.

This is a database of statistical edges I have collected over time, with search functionality built in to help discover patterns based on any market conditions, as well as an ‘Ask the Edge Lab’ engine where you can directly ask a question in plain English about SPX, NDX or BTC (or all three) and get the relevant statistical data back.

For example, I can ask “If Bitcoin holds Tokyo low, SPX sweeps it and then BTC closes London above Tokyo high, what happens during NY?” and the Edge Lab will share precisely what has happened previously in those instances, along with hit rates, MFE, MAE and all sorts of other useful data.

I use this intraday/intraweek and it is particularly useful for establishing your bias alongside price-action, as well as setting TPs/SLs. 

Enjoy 🤝

tweets.text:
Venice burned about $1.06M of $VVV in October, its biggest regular month so far. 

The bad news is that total supply is still going up, because more new VVV came out in October than got burned.

However...

That math changes soon in January 2027. 

Right now about 19K new VVV hits the market every day from staking rewards and unlocks. 

Most of the scheduled unlocks end on January 1, so that drops to around 6K a day. If burns stay the same, they cover about a quarter of new supply instead of 7.5%, roughly 3x the impact.

Usage is growing fast too. Venice says @AskVenice went from about 250B to over 1T AI tokens (the small chunks of text AI reads and writes) a day in October.

There are two catches though, and both are bad for holders.

1, Usage isn't the same as paid revenue. Even after January, burns need to grow about 4x before supply really shrinks.

2. VVV holders don't own any of Venice's revenue. The company decides how much to burn, and it can change that.

So I'm cautiously bullish, but only for a window. 

Investor tokens start unlocking in July 2027 and could add up to ~6K VVV a day, which is about as much as all the new supply after January. 

So January to July is the six months where burns face the least new supply they'll see for years, and if they can't catch up to it then, I don't think they ever will.

$SNAP Earnings: Back To The Free Perpetual Option Price

Market Cap: ~$9B | Earnings Reaction: -13%

$SNAP is back to roughly $5.20, the same price at which I initially recommended it, further reinforcing my original thesis: this is essentially a free perpetual option on Evan Spiegel finally making the right decisions.

Yesterday’s earnings showed revenue growth of 14%, adjusted EBITDA up 110%, and improving profitability and cash flow. On the negative side, advertising growth remains weak at 4%, stock-based compensation is still too high, and Spiegel has yet to make the strategic changes I want to see.

With 977 million monthly active users, $SNAP trades at just $9 per monthly user. Even comparing daily active users, the valuation gap is enormous:

$SNAP: ~$18 per daily user
$RDDT: ~$151 per daily user
$META: ~$442 per daily user

If $SNAP were trading at a $30 billion valuation, I would avoid it all together. But at just $9 billion, with improving profitability and cash generation, it’s hard for me to see the stock going substantially lower from here.

Unlike many growth companies, $SNAP doesn’t need to invent a new business or find hundreds of millions of new users. It already has nearly a billion users. It simply needs to monetize them better, something $META has beautifully demonstrated can be achieved through AI.

Evan Spiegel also needs to have the same realization Mark Zuckerberg eventually had about the metaverse: spending billions on a project doesn’t necessarily mean it will become a profitable business. The difference is that Specs actually have compelling real-world applications, but $SNAP needs a partner to share the costs, risks and development.

I believe Spiegel knows this. The day he announces a serious partner that de-risks Specs, I wouldn’t be surprised to see $SNAP jump 20% or more in a single day. And that’s just one of several possible catalysts, alongside better advertising monetization, reduced stock-based compensation and improved capital allocation.

None of these changes seems like a particularly tall order. Until then, perhaps $5-$6 is exactly where the stock deserves to trade. We’re essentially waiting for something to change, and if it does, the upside could be substantial. If it doesn’t, I believe the low valuation and enormous user base provide a meaningful margin of safety.

I recommended taking some profits when the stock rose from $5 towards $7 without any news to justify the move. Now that we’re back near $5, I believe the entry point is attractive again.

My Action: I’m Buying the Dip.

We’re starting to see measurable improvements in $SNAP ’s financial performance, and I believe the market’s 12% punishment following earnings was too harsh.

Of course, nothing is guaranteed. Spiegel could continue making the same mistakes, and the stock could remain depressed for years, but it’s hard to justify valuing a company with more than 900 million monthly users at less than $9 billion.

That’s what I mean by a free perpetual option. Heads, I win big. Tails, I barely lose.

$STAA: The Turnaround Continues

Market Cap: ~$1.5B | Yesterday Earnings Reaction: +9% | Last Month: +30%

For those unfamiliar with $STAA, STAAR Surgical is the global leader in implantable lenses for vision correction, an alternative to LASIK that doesn’t require removing corneal tissue. The company has a relatively strong moat, built on proprietary Collamer technology, regulatory approvals, decades of clinical data and relationships with eye surgeons. When it comes to your eyes, you’re not going to put something inside them that hasn’t been tested in other people’s eyes for at least 5 to 10 years. Competitors have faced safety problems with implantable lenses in the past that where considered “the next big thing”, making STAAR’s long clinical track record a substantial competitive advantage.

I initially recommended $STAA at $17.50, following the proposed $30.75 acquisition by Alcon, which was opposed by Broadwood Partners, a hedge fund owning approximately 30% of the company, on the grounds that the offer was too opportunistic.

Yesterday’s earnings further reinforced my investment thesis. Revenue reached $83.4M, representing 21% underlying growth, with China up 31% and Europe up 31%. Adjusted EBITDA improved to $14.4M, net income reached $5.6M, and cash increased to $206M with zero debt. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached $270.5M and adjusted EBITDA $58.8M. Management also authorized a $50M share buyback.

Gross margins remain under pressure at 70.9%, but management expects improvement beginning in Q4 and continuing into 2027.

The important story is how much the business has changed since the acquisition offer. If you’ve followed my tweets, you know that the underlying business has improved substantially. I would argue that the company’s situation today is many times better than when the $30.75 offer was made and subsequently rejected.

Just before the latest earnings, Steve Cohen’s Point72 acquired approximately 5% of the company at around $29 per share. Despite the stock’s recent 45% rally, we’re only now back to roughly the price at which Point72 established its position.

With a strong balance sheet, recovering profitability and growing demand for its products, I believe there’s considerably more upside. It’s not hard for me to see $STAA reaching $50 per share with patience.

Following its 45% rise, $STAA is now my second-largest position.

For my full research report and original investment thesis, see the tweet below.

The NASDAQ has already given back all of its post-midterm gains, down another 3% today.

Similar thing happened in 2018.

Lot of exuberance following the midterms in 2018 (SPX rallied 2% the next day), then 3 major events caused the market to sell-off into December.

1) A Hawkish Fed: In October 2018, Fed Chairman Jerome Powell remarked that interest rates were still a long way from neutral, signaling to investors that the Fed would continue tightening monetary policy into 2019 regardless of cooling economic data. This triggered severe liquidity fears and widespread panic selling.

This is similar to today in that the market is pricing in 2 more rate hikes despite the sell-off we have seen in tech.

2) Escalating U.S.–China Trade War : Just before and after the midterms, a flood of major multinational companies (including Caterpillar, 3M, and Ford) warned that rising tariff costs were eating into their profit margins and disrupting global supply chains.

This is similar to today as tariffs have had major inflationary effects and is one of the reasons why the Fed has to remain hawkish.

3) Tech Valuation Reversals: The technology sector, which had been the primary engine driving the multi-year bull market, abruptly reversed course in late 2018. We also had the FAANG slump in which major tech giants faced severe regulatory scrutiny over antitrust and data privacy concerns (such as Facebook's controversies).

This is similar to today as the AI trade has taken quite the breather with AI fears mounting.

History does not always repeat itself, but it does often rhyme.

The market is treating a Dem sweep as an existential threat to AI infrastructure. It’s not.

Data centres can (and already are) being built outside the US. Hyperscalers have major footprints and active expansions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Canada and LatAm. Power, speed of permitting and cost drive site selection more than pure US policy.

If domestic buildouts slow, capital will simply reallocate. Global AI compute demand doesn’t disappear because Northern Virginia or Texas gets harder to permit. Latency-sensitive training prefers concentrated clusters, but inference, regional capacity and a large share of workloads work fine abroad.

The nutty part is the indiscriminate selling of the whole growth stock complex. High-quality, FCF-positive AI names and infrastructure software companies with multi-year visibility are getting lumped in with pure high-beta, negative-FCF builders that actually do have financing and execution risk. 

Policy friction in one country ≠ the end of the AI buildout.

International optionality is real.

There were about 10,000 new venture funds started between 2019 and 2022.

They have not done well.

That money went deep and wide. Little seed groups everywhere.

What happened? Markets shifted. Returns compressed. Competition exploded.

Most of those funds won't raise a second fund.

That's the reality of venture: It looks easier than it is.

From the outside, it's "just invest in startups." From the inside, it's judgment, timing, relationships, and conviction through the J-curve.

The funds that survive will be the ones that differentiate. That built real advantages.

Not the ones that just showed up with capital.

tweets.text:
hard to articulate what i'm thinking here after Tuesday, but i'll give it a shot because i think it's important to understand the seismic shift occurring within both political parties in the US:

Democrats fucked themselves up in the lead up to 2024 because they over-rotated on stupid social issues as a way to stand against Trump. they thought this was legitimately their best strategy and it became their entire brand to a lot of people

ofc, it was a disaster. most people don't mind what others do in their own homes, but they don't want things forced down their throats

but what's interesting about the big wins on Tuesday is the Democrats didn't win (or even run) on these issues. though their opponents on the right tried to saddle them with that baggage, it simply didn't work

the messages which broke through were around 1) affordability, 2) ending the Iran war (which has also harmed affordability), 3) addressing somewhat vague concerns around AI-related job loss (most tangibly observed in unmitigated data center build out), and 4) stemming the substantial observable corruption within the Trump administration

social issues were almost completely absent from the Democratic platform. further, the winning platform also didn't really originate meaningfully from the traditional DNC elites. it bubbled up through a lot of younger upstart candidates, many of whom could seriously be credible as candidates for POTUS in 2028

so it's likely the Democratic talent vacuum has ended, and the Republican talent vacuum is now beginning

as a result, it's quite possible that Democrats WON'T have to go further left on social issues to recruit the votes needed to win POTUS in 2028. IF they can hold on this, then it also simultaneously makes their platform more attractive to relatively centrist Republicans who are also fed up with all of the aforementioned issues

so if Dems don't fuck up on social issues and on immigration (i.e., they need to have a credibly strong immigration policy), then they don't need the extreme left to win anymore

in isolation, this seems like it would break the two party system, but the response will be that the Republican Party moves further to the left on some issues. nativist and race-driven platforms won't work because they are inherently exclusionary. most normal people not on this site in 2026 are also not driven by racial factors in their voting decisions

so, tl;dr- big shifts are coming to both parties. Democrats will actually move more centrist on social issues while becoming more meaningfully progressive on economic issues. Republicans tbd, but they also probably move more towards the center back to economic issues the working class cares about (not just social issues)

like it or not, the race for 2028 starts now 🇺🇸

The current $VVV chart is extremely reminiscent of the May-June distribution pattern, with sudden strong bursts getting completely retraced and printing lower highs (see yesterday's brutal pump-and-dump).

Last time, there was a perfect support/resistance level retest at $10 which gave an entry for a +250% move

The same scenario here could be a retest of $18 for example.

After such a wild multiple (up 30x bottom to top), I would normally be very bearish on the token but they are now buying back $50k+ worth of tokens daily and the size of the buybacks has been going up only, so yeah it makes sense for people to pick VVV as an alt long when they go want to go risk-on...

But for now, the chart remains bearish, and it's probably safer to keep this bias until there's something constructive showing up.

The new UX is the API. The new user is an agent. For decades, the best product builders were the ones who understood humans better than anyone else.

Building great software meant having a really good intuition for UX. Will people know where to click? Can they find the right action? Is the product intuitive?

A lot of the best builders developed that intuition as teenagers building websites, then spent years learning what makes software easy to use.

But now we're building for agents, and it's a completely different skill set. Take booking a business trip. For humans, you build a nice interface to search flights, pick a hotel, add things to your calendar and submit expenses.

For an agent, none of that matters. What matters is whether it can figure out which APIs to call, understand the parameters, handle errors, and complete the whole thing without getting stuck halfway through.

An API can make perfect sense to an engineer and still be terrible for an agent. So for example, imagine an API where creating a calendar event, inviting attendees, booking a meeting room and setting permissions are four separate operations. Perfectly logical from an engineering perspective. But now an agent has to discover the right sequence, understand dependencies, handle partial failures and clean up if something goes wrong. Why not let it express the entire intent in one call and have the system handle the rest?

I think we're going to see a new generation of product builders who have incredible intuition for how agents think, what confuses them, and how to make software that they can actually use.

tweets.full_text:
The new UX is the API. The new user is an agent. For decades, the best product builders were the ones who understood humans better than anyone else.

Building great software meant having a really good intuition for UX. Will people know where to click? Can they find the right action? Is the product intuitive?

A lot of the best builders developed that intuition as teenagers building websites, then spent years learning what makes software easy to use.

But now we're building for agents, and it's a completely different skill set. Take booking a business trip. For humans, you build a nice interface to search flights, pick a hotel, add things to your calendar and submit expenses.

For an agent, none of that matters. What matters is whether it can figure out which APIs to call, understand the parameters, handle errors, and complete the whole thing without getting stuck halfway through.

An API can make perfect sense to an engineer and still be terrible for an agent. So for example, imagine an API where creating a calendar event, inviting attendees, booking a meeting room and setting permissions are four separate operations. Perfectly logical from an engineering perspective. But now an agent has to discover the right sequence, understand dependencies, handle partial failures and clean up if something goes wrong. Why not let it express the entire intent in one call and have the system handle the rest?

I think we're going to see a new generation of product builders who have incredible intuition for how agents think, what confuses them, and how to make software that they can actually use.

It's a new kind of product empathy (let's call it agent empathy, haha!)
